'''A. Francis Stewart''' is an [[Australians|Australian]] [[biochemist]], developmental biologist, and genetic engineer. He is an emeritus senior professor at [[TU Dresden|Technische Universität Dresden]].

Stewart's research focused on [[epigenetics]] and genome engineering, mainly in mammalian systems. His work in genetic engineering was acknowledged by the [[International Society for Transgenic Technologies]] Prize in 2010. He was elected a member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] (EMBO) in 2007 and [[Academia Europaea]] in 2020.

==Education and career==
Stewart earned a [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] degree in [[Biochemistry]] in 1981 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in 1985, both from the [[University of New South Wales]], where he sequenced and investigated cloned [[DNA]]s encoding bovine milk proteins in Tony Mackinlay's laboratory.<ref name=cv>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Stewart_Francis/CV|title=A. Francis Stewart - Curriculum Vitae|website=Academia Europea|access-date=June 2, 2025}}</ref> In 1991, he was appointed group leader in the Gene Expression Program at the [[European Molecular Biology Laboratory]] (EMBL) in Heidelberg.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.embl.org/about/info/alumni/blog/2013/07/pluripotency-project-brings-former-group-leaders-back-together/|title=Pluripotency project brings former group leaders back together|website=EMBL|date=19 July 2013 |access-date=June 2, 2025}}</ref> In 2001, he became group leader at the Biotechnology Center (BIOTEC) and chair of [[Genomics]] at Technische Universität Dresden (TU Dresden).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://fis.tu-dresden.de/portal/en/organisations/chair-of-applied-genomics(4803f8f8-b659-46e4-9a1c-94271e137b28).html|title=Chair of Applied Genomics|website=TU Dresden|access-date=June 2, 2025}}</ref> From 2014 to 2016, he was the director at BIOTEC.<ref name=b>{{Cite web|url=https://tu-dresden.de/cmcb/biotec/forschungsgruppen/stewart/group-leader|title=Biotechnology Center–Group Leader|website=TU Dresden|access-date=June 2, 2025}}</ref> He contributed to the expansion of the Tatzberg research campus to include the DFG Center for Regenerative Therapies Dresden (CRTD) Excellence Initiative in 2005,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gepris.dfg.de/gepris/projekt/32725986|title=EXC 168: Center for Regenerative Therapies Dresden (CRTD)|website=DFG|access-date=June 2, 2025}}</ref> and the DFG Physics of Life (PoL) Excellence Initiative in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gepris.dfg.de/gepris/projekt/390729961?language=en|title=EXC 2068: Physics of Life - The Dynamic Organization of Living Matter (PoL)|website=DFG|access-date=June 2, 2025}}</ref>

Stewart co-founded and chaired the biotech company Gene Bridges.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://dev.genebridges.com/gb/company.php|title=Gene Bridges–Company|website=Gene Bridges|access-date=June 2, 2025}}</ref>

==Research==
With Colin Logie, Stewart developed ligand-inducible site-specific recombinases (SSR-LBDs).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Feil |first1=Robert |last2=Wagner |first2=Jürgen |last3=Metzger |first3=Daniel |last4=Chambon |first4=Pierre |title=Regulation of Cre Recombinase Activity by Mutated Estrogen Receptor Ligand-Binding Domains |journal=Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications |date=August 1997 |volume=237 |issue=3 |pages=752–757 |doi=10.1006/bbrc.1997.7124 |pmid=9299439 |bibcode=1997BBRC..237..752F }}</ref> To address the thermal instability of FLP recombinase, he and Frank Buchholz engineered the thermostable variant FLPe.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gaj |first1=Thomas |last2=Sirk |first2=Shannon J. |last3=Barbas |first3=Carlos F. |title=Expanding the scope of site-specific recombinases for genetic and metabolic engineering |journal=Biotechnology and Bioengineering |date=January 2014 |volume=111 |issue=1 |pages=1–15 |doi=10.1002/bit.25096 |pmid=23982993 |pmc=4097888 |bibcode=2014BiotB.111....1G }}</ref>

To support large-scale genome engineering, Stewart and Youming Zhang developed recombineering, a method using λ-Red and/or RecE/RecT-mediated homologous recombination in ''E. coli'', which allows for flexible and precise manipulation of large DNA constructs such as BACs. Building upon this, his lab streamlined the protocol to eliminate unwanted recombination events.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Court |first1=Donald L. |last2=Sawitzke |first2=James A. |last3=Thomason |first3=Lynn C. |title=Genetic Engineering Using Homologous Recombination |journal=Annual Review of Genetics |date=December 2002 |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=361–388 |doi=10.1146/annurev.genet.36.061102.093104 |pmid=12429697 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Copeland |first1=Neal G. |last2=Jenkins |first2=Nancy A. |last3=Court |first3=Donald L. |title=Recombineering: a powerful new tool for mouse functional genomics |journal=Nature Reviews Genetics |date=October 2001 |volume=2 |issue=10 |pages=769–779 |doi=10.1038/35093556 |pmid=11584293 }}</ref>
